categories.description: The week of making, from melt to annealer.

categories.name: Notes from Usuzawa
categories.description: The town, the river and the bottles.

posts.title: The autumn batch came out paler
posts.excerpt: This month’s glass is a shade lighter than summer’s. The reason is a crate of old soda bottles.
posts.content:
This month’s glass is a shade lighter than summer’s. The reason is a crate of old soda bottles.

Where the colour comes from

We never tint the glass. Its green is simply the green of the bottles we melt, and the mix changes with what the town throws away.

In September a café on the harbour closed and gave us forty crates of pale soda bottles. The October melt took on their light.

Keeping a batch together

Pieces from one melt share one colour, so we keep sets from the same week. If you are adding to a set, tell us when you bought it.

The bottles decide the green; we only listen.

Noe Kanemura

posts.title: A night in the annealer
posts.excerpt: Every piece we make spends its first night in a small kiln, cooling slowly. Without it, glass would crack on its own.
posts.content:
Every piece we make spends its first night in a small kiln, cooling slowly. Without it, glass would crack on its own.

Why glass needs to rest

Hot glass cools faster on the outside than inside, and the difference leaves a strain hidden in the wall.

In the annealer it is held at 480 °C and brought down a few degrees an hour until morning, so the strain eases out.

Opening the door

On Wednesday mornings we open the annealer to Tuesday’s work. It is still the quietest, best moment of the week.

Patience is the last tool on the bench.

Teo Arashiro

posts.title: Caring for handmade glass
posts.excerpt: Handmade glass is not fragile, but it likes a few habits: warm water, a soft cloth and no sudden heat.
posts.content:
Handmade glass is not fragile, but it likes a few habits: warm water, a soft cloth and no sudden heat.

Washing

Hand-wash in warm water with a little soap. Dishwashers are hard on recycled glass and slowly cloud its surface.

Dry with a linen cloth while the glass is still warm, and it will stay bright.

About the bubbles

Small seeds of air are caught in the glass as it is blown. They are part of the material, not a fault.

Use it every day; that is what it is for.

Rin Okabe

posts.title: The shape of a pour
posts.excerpt: How the River Carafe found its narrow waist, after a summer of carafes that dripped.
posts.content:
How the River Carafe found its narrow waist, after a summer of carafes that dripped.

Twenty carafes

The first carafes poured well but were hard to hold when full. We pinched the neck lower, then higher, then lower again.

The waist came last: a soft narrowing where the hand naturally falls.

A clean line

The lip is turned out a little at the very end, so the water leaves it in one line and never runs down the side.

A good pour is quiet.

Noe Kanemura

posts.title: Bottles from the harbour
posts.excerpt: Twice a month we collect bottles from the harbour restaurants. A note on where our glass begins.
posts.content:
Twice a month we collect bottles from the harbour restaurants. A note on where our glass begins.

The Thursday round

Rin drives the small van along the harbour road on alternate Thursdays and fills it with green bottles left in crates by the back doors.

They are washed in the yard, labels soaked off, then crushed in a steel drum.

A town in a glass

Most of what we make has been, at some point, a bottle on a table somewhere in Usuzawa.

We make new things from the town’s old ones.

Rin Okabe

posts.title: Packing a crate
posts.excerpt: Every order leaves in a small wooden crate. Why we still pack by hand, and what we promise if something breaks.
posts.content:
Every order leaves in a small wooden crate. Why we still pack by hand, and what we promise if something breaks.

Paper, husk, wood

Each piece is wrapped in recycled paper, set in rice-husk padding and held so it cannot touch the crate walls.

The crates are made by a carpenter two streets away and can be used again.

If it breaks

It rarely happens, but when it does, send us a photograph. We make a new piece and send it, and you keep the crate.

A crate is the last part of the piece.

Rin Okabe

products.name: Usuzawa Tumbler
products.short: A straight, slightly thick-walled tumbler in old bottle green, made for water at the table every day.
products.description:
A straight, slightly thick-walled tumbler in old bottle green, made for water at the table every day.

Blown into a wooden mould so each one keeps the same height, then finished by hand at the rim. The base is a little heavier so it sits quietly.

Every piece is hand-made, so size and colour vary slightly from the photograph. Small bubbles are part of the glass.

products.name: Reed Stem Wine Glass
products.short: A round bowl on a long, thin stem, drawn out by hand like a reed at the water’s edge.
products.description:
A round bowl on a long, thin stem, drawn out by hand like a reed at the water’s edge.

The bowl, stem and foot are made in one sitting by two makers working together. A few small seeds (bubbles) in the stem are part of the glass.

Every piece is hand-made, so size and colour vary slightly from the photograph. Small bubbles are part of the glass.

products.name: River Carafe
products.short: A tall carafe with a narrow neck and a soft waist, for water or cold tea on the table.
products.description:
A tall carafe with a narrow neck and a soft waist, for water or cold tea on the table.

The neck is pinched while the glass is still soft, so it pours in a clean line and the carafe is easy to hold with one hand.

Every piece is hand-made, so size and colour vary slightly from the photograph. Small bubbles are part of the glass.

products.name: Shallow Tide Bowl
products.short: A wide, shallow bowl that holds the light like the tide on sand. For summer fruit, salads or chilled noodles.
products.description:
A wide, shallow bowl that holds the light like the tide on sand. For summer fruit, salads or chilled noodles.

Cut from a sheet of our own glass and slumped slowly over a ceramic mould in the kiln, so the rim keeps a soft, uneven line.

Every piece is hand-made, so size and colour vary slightly from the photograph. Small bubbles are part of the glass.

products.name: Bottle Green Bud Vase
products.short: A small vase with a narrow mouth for one stem: a branch of plum, a grass, a single late rose.
products.description:
A small vase with a narrow mouth for one stem: a branch of plum, a grass, a single late rose.

The deepest green we make, from the darkest bottles we collect. The walls are thicker at the foot so the vase stands steady with water in it.

Every piece is hand-made, so size and colour vary slightly from the photograph. Small bubbles are part of the glass.

products.name: Morning Pitcher
products.short: A generous pitcher with an applied handle, for water with lemon, cold barley tea or a bunch of flowers.
products.description:
A generous pitcher with an applied handle, for water with lemon, cold barley tea or a bunch of flowers.

The handle is pulled from a separate gather of glass and set on while both are hot. It takes two of us and one long breath.

Every piece is hand-made, so size and colour vary slightly from the photograph. Small bubbles are part of the glass.

products.name: Sake Pair
products.short: Two small cups for cold sake, one a little paler than the other, in a paulownia box.
products.description:
Two small cups for cold sake, one a little paler than the other, in a paulownia box.

Made from the same gather and blown one after the other, so the pair is never quite identical. For cold sake, plum wine or a mouthful of water.

Every piece is hand-made, so size and colour vary slightly from the photograph. Small bubbles are part of the glass.
